chapter_title: Concrete Placement, Finishing, Texturing, and Curing

sections.title: Paving Equipment
sections.summary: Paver-finishing machines handle mainline pavement and large fillets; handwork covers small areas. Heavy pavers (slipform) and light pavers (bridge deck finishers, clary/truss/roller screeds) are both used, with light machines allowed only when the contractor demonstrates satisfactory results.
sections.body: Paver-finishing machines accomplish concrete paving for mainline pavement and large fillets; handwork areas are those too small to use a machine. Heavy and light pavers are used for machine paving; slipform pavers are heavy machines. Only use light-weight machines, such as bridge deck finishers, clary screeds, truss screeds, or roller screeds if the contractor can show that they can produce satisfactory pavement with this type of equipment.
key_points: Machine paving covers mainline/large fillets; handwork covers areas too small for machines
Slipform pavers are the heavy-machine category
Light machines (bridge deck finishers, clary/truss/roller screeds) require contractor demonstration of satisfactory results
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the appropriate paving equipment class for a given pavement area.

sections.title: Slipform Pavers
sections.summary: Slipform pavers can stretch to 14-15 m (45-50 ft) but are commonly used at 8-11 m (25-37.5 ft) width, are typically used for airfield pavement >=200 mm (8 in.) thick, and provide the consolidation needed for deep-lift concrete via self-propelled, four-track, variable-speed vibratory equipment carrying a concrete head.
sections.body: Slipform pavers can be used in side form applications by stretching the paver width beyond the forms. Slipform pavers can stretch to 14 or 15 m (45 to 50 ft), depending upon model and available attachments, but most are commonly used at 8 to 11 m (25 to 37.5 ft) width. Slipform pavers are usually used for airfield concrete pavement that is 200 mm (8 in.) or more in thickness, and provide the consolidation required for deep lift concrete pavement. Common elements of the slipform paver include: self-propelled with four tracks; generally weigh at least 3,280 kg/m (2,200 lb/ft) of paving lane width; variable-speed hydraulically controlled internal vibrators; ability to carry a head of concrete in front of the screed; continuous auger or hydraulic plow-pans to distribute concrete in front of the screed; and finishing attachments.
key_points: Typical operating width 8-11 m (25-37.5 ft); can stretch to 14-15 m (45-50 ft)
Typically used for airfield pavement >=200 mm (8 in.) thick, providing deep-lift consolidation
Self-propelled, four-track, weighing >= 3,280 kg/m (2,200 lb/ft) of lane width, with hydraulic variable-speed vibrators
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and sizing slipform paving equipment for thicker airfield concrete pavement.

sections.title: Manual Paving
sections.summary: Labor-intensive manual paving is typically limited to small areas such as fillets.
sections.body: Labor-intensive manual paving is typically carried out only for small areas such as fillets. Manual placement lacks the consolidation and finishing consistency of machine paving, so it is reserved for geometry too small or irregular for a paver.
key_points: Manual paving is reserved for small areas (e.g., fillets) where machine paving is impractical
Manual paving is labor-intensive compared to slipform or bridge deck machine paving
sections.applicability: Applies to small, irregular areas not suited to machine paving.

sections.title: Differences Between Slipform and Bridge Deck Paving Machines
sections.summary: Bridge deck pavers have lower production capacity but are most economical/maneuverable in wide (>12 m/40 ft) or geometrically constrained areas; their single-vibrator zigzag consolidation is less uniform than slipform's uniformly spaced, single-direction vibrators, and mixture designs are not interchangeable between the two paving types.
sections.body: The differences between slipform and bridge deck paving machines are summarized as follows: the bridge deck paver production capacity is significantly less than a slipform paver; the bridge deck paver is most economical when paving lanes wider than 12 m (40 ft) and in geometrically constrained areas, capable of placing concrete up to 15 m (50 ft) wide; a bridge deck paver is more mobile/maneuverable and may be used in constrained areas such as cross-taxiways or restricted aprons. A major consolidation difference: the single vibrator of a bridge deck paver consolidates by plowing transversely across the truss, and combined with forward travel, the concrete is plowed in a zigzag pattern; for a constant radius of action, depending on forward speed, the vibration energy and coarse aggregate distribution may not be as uniform as slipform's uniformly spaced, single-direction-plowing vibrators. Vibrators on bridge deck pavers may have smaller offset weights allowing higher frequencies than desired, increasing the potential for disrupting the air void system and durability problems; and concrete mixtures are uniquely designed for fixed form paving -- slipform paver mixtures do not work for fixed form paving and vice versa.
key_points: Bridge deck pavers: lower production capacity, most economical for lanes > 12 m (40 ft) wide or constrained geometry, up to 15 m (50 ft) placement width
Bridge deck paver consolidation (zigzag, single transverse vibrator) is less uniform than slipform's
Higher bridge deck paver vibrator frequencies risk disrupting the air-void system
Slipform and fixed-form (bridge deck) mixture designs are NOT interchangeable
sections.applicability: Applies to choosing between slipform and bridge deck paving machines based on lane width and site geometry.

sections.title: Critical Factors for Concrete Paving
sections.summary: Critical paving factors: good, trimmed/compacted grade; stringline management; continuous concrete supply; consistent workability; well-maintained/properly operated equipment; controlled density/vibration; and, most importantly, a skilled and dedicated crew.
sections.body: The following are critical factors affecting concrete paving: a good grade for paving, trimmed and compacted to specification; stringline management (monitor and maintain at regular intervals); continuous supply of concrete to the paver; consistent concrete workability; well-maintained paving equipment; proper operation of paving equipment; controlled density of concrete (just the right level of vibration to consolidate and provide enough surface fines for a tight finish); and, most importantly, a skilled and dedicated crew.
key_points: Critical factors: grade quality, stringline management, continuous concrete supply, consistent workability
Well-maintained, properly operated equipment and controlled vibration/density
Most importantly: a skilled and dedicated crew
sections.applicability: Serves as the top-level checklist of factors governing successful concrete paving.

sections.title: Concrete Delivery at the Site
sections.summary: Before/during delivery: inspect and clean the grade, verify stringline elevations, deposit concrete within a reasonable time of mixing water addition (leaving time for consolidation/strike-off/finishing before initial set), use slightly higher slump when pulling off headers, prefer agitator trucks, and maintain consistent delivery to avoid paver stop-start.
sections.body: Before and during concrete delivery, the following should be considered: inspect the grade for acceptance before depositing concrete, removing loose debris and repairing any base damage; verify string line elevations; deposit concrete on grade within a reasonable time after the addition of mixing water, leaving time remaining for consolidation, strike-off, and finishing before initial set; when pulling slipform pavers off headers, use a slightly higher slump concrete to facilitate hand consolidation and finishing; encourage the use of agitator trucks, which usually provide more uniform concrete placement and minimize segregation; and maintain consistent delivery of concrete to minimize paver stopping and starting -- if paving stops to wait for concrete from the batch plant, use additional trucks or reduce paver speed.
key_points: Inspect/clean the grade and verify stringline elevations before depositing concrete
Leave enough time after water addition for consolidation, strike-off, and finishing before initial set
Use slightly higher slump concrete when pulling slipform pavers off headers
Consistent delivery (agitator trucks, added trucks, or reduced paver speed) minimizes stop-start paving
sections.applicability: Applies to managing concrete delivery logistics to keep the paving operation continuous.

sections.title: Concrete Placement
sections.summary: Deposit concrete close to and uniformly in front of the paver without overloading one side or disturbing base/steel/dowels/forms; dumping directly in front of the paver keeps a consistent concrete head but risks disturbing the base and rushing dowel basket placement/verification, so a full-time inspector may be needed.
sections.body: Acceptable concrete placement practices include: depositing concrete close to and uniformly in front of the paver or front spreader, taking care to minimize disturbance to the base, embedded steel, dowel bars, and side forms; placing concrete so one side of the paving lane is not overloaded; in formed areas, placing concrete as close as possible to its final position to minimize segregation potential; dumping on grade (controlling the rate via the tailgate opening -- spreading in front of a paver with an end loader is poor practice) or onto belt placers/side-loading spreaders. Dumping directly in front of pavers/spreaders keeps a concrete head easily maintained in front of the machine auger, but disadvantages include: trucks backing into the paver may disturb the compacted granular base; and dowel baskets must be placed just ahead of the paver, which may not allow time to verify dowel bar alignment or that baskets are securely fastened -- a full-time inspector may be required to check dowel bar placement and alignment when baskets are placed just ahead of the paver, and stringlines may need to be broken on at least one side to allow trucks to back in and pull away. When using a belt placer, swing the belt back and forth to maintain a uniform concrete head, backing up the placer if the paver is low on concrete. When using a spreader, do not advance it more than 7.5 m (25 ft) ahead of the paver, to allow timely adjustment of the concrete head. The paver operator must control the level of concrete in the grout box by raising/lowering the strike-off blade as needed. To reduce dowel bar misalignment from the forward-moving concrete head: deposit small amounts of concrete carefully over pre-positioned baskets fastened to the base, and do not dump concrete by trucks directly on basket assemblies.
key_points: Deposit concrete close to and uniformly in front of the paver; minimize disturbance to base, steel, dowel bars, and forms
Dumping directly in front of the paver risks disturbing the base and rushes dowel basket placement -- may require a full-time dowel inspector
Spreader advance limit: no more than 7.5 m (25 ft) ahead of the paver
Reduce dowel misalignment: deposit concrete carefully over pre-positioned baskets; never dump trucks directly on basket assemblies
sections.applicability: Applies to placement technique choices (dumping, belt placer, spreader) and their dowel-basket disturbance risk.

sections.title: Concrete Head
sections.summary: Concrete head must be consistent and at the proper height for paver size and concrete mix; a heavier paver is generally smoother since it is less affected by concrete surges.
sections.body: Concrete head must be consistent and of proper height for the paver size and concrete mix. A heavier paver generally produces a smoother concrete pavement since it is less affected by surges of concrete coming into the paver.
key_points: Concrete head height must be consistent and matched to the paver size and mix
Heavier pavers produce smoother pavement because they resist concrete-surge effects
sections.applicability: Applies to managing the concrete head maintained in front of the paver during placement.

sections.title: Paver Speed
sections.summary: Slow, constant paver speed yields smooth pavement; speed should match batch plant/delivery capability, avoid frequent stops, and generally run a minimum of 30 m (100 ft) per hour.
sections.body: Slow and constant speed of the paver results in smooth pavements. The rate of placement (speed of the paver) should coincide with the capability of the batch plant and the rate of delivery of concrete to the paver. The paver should not be stopped frequently during the paving operation. Generally, the forward speed should be a minimum of 30 m (100 ft) per hour.
key_points: Slow, constant paver speed produces smoother pavement
Paver speed should match batch plant capability and delivery rate; avoid frequent stops
Minimum forward speed guidance: 30 m (100 ft) per hour
sections.applicability: Applies to setting/monitoring paver forward speed for smoothness.

sections.title: Filler Lane Placement
sections.summary: If pilot lane joints are open >6 mm (0.25 in.) at filler lane time, use backer rod/duct tape/asphalt mastic to prevent mortar seepage causing corner spalls; filler lanes are also prone to cracking from doweled-joint restraint, pilot-lane friction, higher slump, and shorter sawing windows.
sections.body: If pilot lane joints are open wide at the time of filler lane placement, mortar from the filler lane can seep into the joints and result in small corner breaks/spalls; if pilot lane joint widths are greater than 6 mm (0.25 in.), use backer rod, duct tape, or asphalt mastic to cover the joint openings. Although filler lanes may appear reasonably easy to place, the paving contractor must be aware of the potential for cracking within filler lanes because of restraint from: doweled longitudinal joints; friction from pilot lane joint faces; possible use of higher slump concrete (more shrinkage potential); and a shorter window for sawing joints.
key_points: Pilot-lane joint openings > 6 mm (0.25 in.): cover with backer rod, duct tape, or asphalt mastic before filler lane placement
Filler lanes are prone to restraint cracking from doweled joints, pilot-lane friction, higher slump, and a shorter sawing window
sections.applicability: Applies to placing a filler (closure) lane against an already-placed pilot lane.

sections.title: Embedded Steel and Tie-Bar Placement
sections.summary: Embedded steel/mesh is supported on chairs strong enough to resist sagging and worker weight during vibration; before placement, inspectors must verify steel bar diameter, length, epoxy coating integrity, location, elevation, clearance from other steel/dowels, and chair frequency.
sections.body: Use chairs to securely support embedded steel bars or mesh typically used in fillet areas and other odd-shaped panels. Space the chairs close enough to support the steel without sagging. Support tie bars used as embedded steel and positioned around penetrations on chairs within tolerances of the specified elevation. Welded wire fabric must be flat and meet specified elevations within tolerances after fastening to chairs. Supplementary consolidation with spud vibrators is commonly used around wire mesh, so chairs must be strong enough to support the weight of laborers during concrete consolidation. Prior to concrete placement accepted by inspectors, verify the embedded steel bar diameter, length, presence of epoxy coatings, absence of breaks in epoxy, location, elevation, clearance of embedded steel (from other steel or dowel/tie bars at joints), and frequency of chairs.
key_points: Chairs must be spaced close enough to prevent steel/mesh sagging, and strong enough to bear laborer weight during vibration
Pre-placement inspection: bar diameter, length, epoxy coating integrity, location, elevation, clearance, chair frequency
sections.applicability: Applies to embedded steel/tie bar placement, especially in fillets and odd-shaped panels.

sections.title: Tie Bars
sections.summary: Tie bars are not permitted on airfield pavements; use tie bars only for road and street projects.
sections.body: Tie bars are not permitted on airfield pavements. Use tie bars only for road and street projects. This restriction distinguishes tie bars (used at longitudinal joints in non-airfield pavements) from dowel bars, which airfields do use for load transfer.
key_points: Tie bars are PROHIBITED on airfield pavements
Tie bars are used only on road and street projects
sections.applicability: Governs whether tie bars may be used at all, based on facility type (airfield vs. road/street).

sections.title: Dowel Bar Installation
sections.summary: Transverse contraction joint dowels use pre-positioned baskets only (no inserters permitted); longitudinal sawed contraction joint dowels may use baskets but not jammers on heavy-duty pavement; longitudinal construction joint dowel inserters are prohibited entirely (high misalignment/air-pocket risk); and longitudinal construction joint / transverse header dowels use the drill-and-epoxy technique.
sections.body: During dowel bar installation, consider the following: dowel bars at transverse contraction joints are pre-positioned using dowel bar baskets secured to the base -- installing these dowels by dowel inserters attached to the paver, or any other means of inserting dowels into plastic concrete, is NOT permitted; dowel bars at longitudinal sawed contraction joints can be pre-positioned using basket assemblies, but cannot be injected using a dowel bar jammer on airfield or other heavy-duty pavement; dowel bar inserters are prohibited at longitudinal construction joints due to the high potential for misalignment and undesirable air pockets; and dowel bars at longitudinal construction joints and transverse headers are installed using a drill and epoxy technique, with holes drilled into vertical edges.
key_points: Transverse contraction joint dowels: pre-positioned baskets ONLY -- inserters NOT permitted
Longitudinal sawed contraction joint dowels: baskets allowed; dowel bar jammers NOT allowed on heavy-duty pavement
Longitudinal construction joint dowel inserters are PROHIBITED (misalignment/air-pocket risk)
Longitudinal construction joints and transverse headers: drill-and-epoxy technique into vertical edges
sections.applicability: Governs the permitted dowel-bar installation method by joint type -- central to avoiding load-transfer defects.

sections.title: Dowel Bar Alignment
sections.summary: Dowel bar alignment must be checked regularly since misalignment significantly affects performance; Table 8-1 lists misalignment types and their performance impact, and Figure 8-1 illustrates them. The following subsections give specific installation items.
sections.body: Dowel bar alignment is a critical item and must be checked on a regular basis. Dowel misalignment has a significant effect on pavement performance. Table 8-1 lists the types of dowel bar misalignment and their impact on performance (horizontal translation, longitudinal translation, and vertical translation each affect load transfer only; vertical translation also causes spalling; horizontal skew and vertical skew each cause spalling, cracking, AND affect load transfer). Figure 8-1 illustrates these types of misalignments. Important dowel installation items follow in the subsections below.
key_points: Dowel alignment must be checked regularly -- misalignment significantly affects performance
Table 8-1: 5 misalignment types (horizontal/longitudinal/vertical translation, horizontal/vertical skew) and their spalling/cracking/load-transfer impacts
Figure 8-1 illustrates the misalignment categories
tables: Table 8-1: Types of Dowel Bar Misalignment and Impact on Performance
sections.applicability: Applies to inspecting and interpreting dowel bar misalignment and its performance consequences.

sections.title: Typical Alignment Specifications
sections.summary: Typical dowel bar alignment tolerances: 10 mm/m (1/8 in./ft) or less out of alignment vertically and horizontally; 15 mm (5/8 in.) or less horizontal/longitudinal translation; 13 mm (1/2 in.) or less vertical translation.
sections.body: Typical dowel bar alignment specifications: 10 mm/m (1/8 in./ft) or less out of alignment in the vertical and horizontal plane; 15 mm (5/8 in.) or less horizontal or longitudinal translation; and 13 mm (1/2 in.) or less vertical translation.
key_points: Skew tolerance: 10 mm/m (1/8 in./ft) or less, vertical and horizontal plane
Horizontal/longitudinal translation tolerance: 15 mm (5/8 in.) or less
Vertical translation tolerance: 13 mm (1/2 in.) or less
sections.applicability: Provides the typical numeric dowel bar alignment tolerances used for CQC inspection acceptance.

sections.title: Basket Assembly Stations
sections.summary: Verify that dowel basket assemblies are centered at the intended joint locations.
sections.body: Verify the assemblies to ensure they are centered at joint locations. Off-station baskets shift the dowel bars away from their intended location relative to the sawn joint, undermining load transfer at that joint.
key_points: Verify dowel basket assemblies are centered at their intended joint stations
Station accuracy is verified before concrete placement, alongside overall basket alignment checks
sections.applicability: Applies to checking basket-assembly station accuracy before concrete placement.

sections.title: Dowel Bars at Longitudinal Joints
sections.summary: Inspect bars to confirm the specified clearance from the ends of transverse joint dowel bars is maintained.
sections.body: Inspect bars to ensure the specified clearance from the ends of transverse joint dowel bars is maintained.
key_points: Verify the specified end-clearance between longitudinal-joint dowels and transverse-joint dowel ends
sections.applicability: Applies to inspecting dowel bar clearance at longitudinal joints near their intersection with transverse joints.

sections.title: Reduce Restraint at Slab Corners
sections.summary: Position longitudinal-joint dowel bars at least 150 mm (6 in.), preferably 300 mm (12 in.), away from the ends of transverse-joint dowel bars to reduce restraint at slab corners.
sections.body: To reduce restraint at slab corners, position dowel bars at longitudinal joints at least 150 mm (6 in.) and preferably 300 mm (12 in.) away from the ends of dowel bars in the transverse joints.
key_points: Longitudinal-joint dowel offset from transverse-joint dowel ends: >= 150 mm (6 in.) minimum, 300 mm (12 in.) preferred
sections.applicability: Applies to laying out dowel bars near slab corners where longitudinal and transverse joints intersect.

sections.title: Dowel Baskets
sections.summary: Securely fasten baskets to the base: clips are generally adequate on stabilized base, but long stakes are required on granular/open-graded bases.
sections.body: Securely fasten baskets to the base. Clips are generally adequate when fastening a basket to stabilized base; long stakes are required to securely fasten baskets in granular and open graded bases.
key_points: Clips are generally adequate for basket fastening on stabilized base
Long stakes are required for basket fastening on granular/open-graded bases
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the correct basket-fastening hardware for the base type.

sections.title: Longitudinal Dowel Basket Wires
sections.summary: Crimp basket wires instead of cutting; crimping reduces cross-sectional area while maintaining basket stability.
sections.body: Crimp wires instead of cutting. Crimping reduces cross-sectional area while maintaining basket stability.
key_points: Crimp basket wires (do not cut) to reduce cross-sectional area while retaining basket stability
sections.applicability: Applies to detailing/releasing longitudinal dowel basket wires before paving.

sections.title: Verify Dowel Bar Alignment
sections.summary: Verify dowel alignment by exposing dowels in plastic concrete, coring over dowel ends, using a magnetic rebar cover meter, or nondestructive testing (e.g., GPR).
sections.body: Verify alignment by: exposing dowels in plastic concrete; coring over dowel bar ends; using a magnetic rebar cover meter; or nondestructive testing such as GPR.
key_points: Verification methods: exposing dowels in plastic concrete, coring over dowel ends, magnetic rebar cover meter, GPR
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting a dowel alignment verification method during or after placement.

sections.title: Prior to Paving
sections.summary: Inspect dowel bars for breaks in the epoxy coating; use field kits to cover exposed steel at basket welds/coating chips, and inspect form release oil/de-bonding agent coverage before placement if specified.
sections.body: Inspect dowel bars for breaks in the epoxy coating. Field kits are used to cover exposed dowel bar steel at basket welds and chips in the coating. If a light coat of form release oil or other de-bonding agent is specified, inspect the coverage before concrete placement.
key_points: Inspect for epoxy coating breaks; use field repair kits at basket welds/coating chips
Inspect form release oil / de-bonding agent coverage before placement, if specified
sections.applicability: Applies to final dowel bar inspection immediately before concrete placement.

sections.title: Basket Versus Inserted Dowels
sections.summary: Baskets use a method specification (positive tie-in to subbase, inspected basket stability/alignment before placement, possible covermeter/GPR checks of first joints); inserted dowels cannot be inspected before placement, so misalignment is only discoverable after the concrete hardens, and specifications often lack inspection detail for inserted dowels.
sections.body: A method specification is typically used for dowel baskets: positive tie-in to subbase is specified; inspection of basket stability and dowel alignment is performed before concrete placement; and dowel placement (depth) for the first few joints per day may be checked using a covermeter or GPR. For inserted dowels, prior inspection is not possible; as a result, the contractor takes a risk because a check of dowel misalignment is only possible after concrete has hardened. The dowel placement (depth) for the first few joints of the day must still be inspected using a covermeter. Also, there is typically not enough guidance in specifications for inspection of inserted dowels -- the contractor should raise this issue at the pre-bid meeting if the inserted dowel technique will be used.
key_points: Baskets: method-specified with pre-placement inspection of tie-in, stability, and alignment
Inserted dowels: NO pre-placement inspection possible -- misalignment discoverable only after hardening (contractor risk)
First-few-joints-per-day depth checks via covermeter/GPR apply to both methods
Raise inserted-dowel inspection-guidance gaps at the pre-bid meeting if that technique will be used
sections.applicability: Compares the inspectability and risk profile of basket-based vs. inserted dowel installation.

sections.title: Dowel Bars at Construction Joints
sections.summary: Construction joint dowels use the drill-and-epoxy-grout procedure (side-injected prohibited on airfields), installed once the concrete can support drilling without excessive chipping; key steps are gang drilling, slight hole oversize (3-6 mm/0.125-0.25 in.), depth spot-checks, back-injecting epoxy while twisting the dowel in, optional retention disks, coverage inspection, and oiling (not greasing) exposed ends.
sections.body: Install dowel bars at construction joints using the drill and epoxy grout procedure. Side injected dowel bars are prohibited on airfield pavements. Install dowel bars after the concrete has cured sufficiently to allow: the new pavement to support drilling equipment weight; and hole drilling without excessive chipping and spalling (>12.5 mm [0.5 in.]) or beyond the diameter of the grout retention disc -- expect minor chipping. Important installation items: use gang drills to simultaneously drill several holes; slightly over-size holes, about 3 to 6 mm (1/8 to 1/4 in.) larger than the dowel bar diameter; spot-check drilled hole depth to ensure dowels are nominally inserted halfway; inject epoxy at the back of the drilled holes and twist the dowel as it is pushed in (applying epoxy by hand to the dowel before insertion is PROHIBITED); grout retention disks may be used to prevent epoxy from flowing out; inspect dowel bars to verify adequacy of epoxy coverage, since proper grouting ensures the dowels bear on a sound interface without voids (otherwise load transfer effectiveness is compromised); and oil the exposed ends of the dowel bars before concrete placement (do NOT use grease).
key_points: Side-injected dowel bars are PROHIBITED on airfield pavements -- drill-and-epoxy-grout only
Hole oversize: 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4 in.) larger than the dowel bar diameter
Chipping/spalling limit around drilled holes: <= 12.5 mm (0.5 in.), or the grout retention disc diameter
Applying epoxy by hand to the dowel before insertion is PROHIBITED -- inject at the back of the hole and twist the dowel in
Oil (never grease) the exposed dowel ends before concrete placement
sections.applicability: Governs the drill-and-epoxy-grout dowel installation procedure required at construction joints.

sections.title: Concrete Consolidation
sections.summary: Slipform paver grout-box vibrators are gang-mounted and hydraulically or electrically driven; inadequate vibration (dead vibrator, high paver speed, poor workability) causes low strength/honeycombing, while over-consolidation (excess frequency, reduced speed without frequency adjustment, poor workability) risks freeze-thaw durability loss; vibrator depth is typically <=100 mm (4 in.), angled 5-10 degrees, spaced per zone of influence, and checked under no load before each paving day.
sections.body: Proper use of internal vibrators is important to properly consolidate the concrete without adversely affecting strength and durability. Slipform pavers consolidate concrete in the grout box using gang-mounted vibrators; for larger pavers, vibrators are hydraulically driven, while electric or hydraulic vibrators may be used for small slipform pavers. Inadequate consolidation results in lower concrete strength and honeycombing, due to a poorly functioning/dead vibrator, paver speed too high, or a mix with poor workability. Over-consolidation can lead to freeze-thaw durability problems if the air void system is adversely altered, due to excessive vibrator frequency, reducing paver forward speed without adjusting vibrator frequency, or a mix with poor workability. Vibrators are generally positioned no more than 100 mm (4 in.) below the finished pavement surface -- setting vibrators too low traps air under the grout box head, causing delamination or blistering. Vibrators are generally positioned at an attitude of 5 to 10 degrees so the angled vibrators plow the concrete as the paver moves forward. Vibrator spacing is a function of the radius of the zone of influence, itself a function of paver speed, vibrator rotor force, and frequency (set by the equipment operator). Before each day of paving, vibratory frequencies and amplitudes must be checked under no load -- large deviations between vibrators indicate poorly functioning vibrators.
key_points: Inadequate consolidation (dead vibrator, high paver speed, poor workability) -> low strength, honeycombing
Over-consolidation (excess frequency, reduced speed w/o frequency adjustment, poor workability) -> freeze-thaw durability risk from altered air-void system
Vibrator depth typically <= 100 mm (4 in.) below finished surface; attitude 5-10 degrees
Check vibratory frequency/amplitude under no load before EACH day of paving
sections.applicability: Applies to setting and verifying paver vibrator parameters for proper consolidation.

sections.title: Verifying Consolidation
sections.summary: Examine test-strip or early-placement cores (relative to vibrator depth/attitude/frequency/spacing/head/speed) for aggregate segregation in vibrator trails, excessive entrapped air, and hardened-density differences.
sections.body: Examine cores drilled in the test strip or initial stages of placement to ensure that, for the paving variables (vibrator depth, attitude angle, frequency under load, spacing, grout box head, and travel speed), the consolidation is acceptable. Examine cores between and in vibrator paths for: evidence of aggregate segregation in vibrator trails; excessive entrapped air; and differences in hardened concrete density.
key_points: Examine cores from the test strip or early placement to verify consolidation adequacy against the set paving variables
Look for aggregate segregation in vibrator trails, excessive entrapped air, and hardened density differences
sections.applicability: Applies to core-based verification of consolidation quality at the start of paving.

sections.title: Vibration for Consolidation
sections.summary: Supplementary vibrators near vertical edges avoid entrapped air; response to the mix should be evaluated on the first paving day/after the test strip, adjusting frequency/speed/depth/spacing to eliminate honeycombing/segregation; smart vibrator systems (continuous frequency monitoring) are recommended, with 6,000-8,000 vpm under load typically giving acceptable consolidation.
sections.body: Slipformed vertical edges should not exhibit excessive entrapped air voids. With slipform and fixed-form pavers, supplementary vibrators may need to be positioned close to vertical edges to ensure adequate consolidation. Evaluate the response of the concrete mixture to vibration on the first day of paving or after test strip construction; eliminate large pockets of entrapped air (honeycombing) and aggregate segregation by changing vibrator frequency, forward travel speed of the paver, vibrator depth, or vibrator spacing. Smart vibrator systems that continuously monitor individual vibrator frequencies during paving are available and recommended, since they allow continuous verification of frequency uniformity. Vibrator frequency in the range of 6,000 to 8,000 vibrations per minute (under load) will usually result in acceptable consolidation for a properly designed mix.
key_points: Add supplementary vibrators near vertical edges to avoid entrapped air voids
Adjustable variables to fix honeycombing/segregation: vibrator frequency, paver speed, vibrator depth, vibrator spacing
Smart vibrator systems (continuous frequency monitoring) are recommended
Typical acceptable vibrator frequency under load: 6,000-8,000 vibrations per minute
sections.applicability: Applies to tuning vibration parameters (including edge consolidation) once paving is underway.

sections.title: Concrete Finishing
sections.summary: Hand finishing corrects unevenness behind the paver and should be minimized -- an ideal mixture/paver setup needs little finishing, water should not be added to assist finishing, and excess surface paste indicates over-watering, over-vibration, low paver speed relative to vibration, or over-finishing.
sections.body: Concrete finishing is a critical step in the paving process, typically hand finishing applied to obtain a smooth surface and correct unevenness behind the paver; finishing efforts should be kept to a minimum, since the correct concrete mixture ideally results in an acceptable surface finish behind the paver -- the surface does not need to be very tight and every small blemish does not need correction. Too much paste at the surface results from too much water applied, over-vibration (high frequency), paver speed too slow for vibratory effort, or over-finishing. The need for concrete finishing is minimized by selecting a workable concrete mixture and properly operating the paving equipment. Excessive hand finishing will work water to the surface and can affect surface smoothness and concrete durability. Problems closing the surface behind the paver are indicative of inadequate grout box volume or concrete setting up in the grout box, low fine-to-coarse aggregate or paste volume, the finishing pan angle needing adjustment, paver speed too high, or vibrators needing adjustment. If water is used to assist finishing, it needs to be fogged (not sprayed) over the surface and not worked in with floats.
key_points: Finishing should be minimized -- a correct mixture and proper paver operation needs little hand finishing
Excess surface paste indicates over-watering, over-vibration, slow paver speed, or over-finishing
Excessive hand finishing works water to the surface, harming smoothness and durability
If water is used, it must be FOGGED (not sprayed) and never worked in with floats
sections.applicability: Applies to concrete finishing technique and diagnosing surface-closure problems behind the paver.

sections.title: Hand Finishing
sections.summary: Excessive hand finishing or adding mortar/water to the surface indicates an undesirable combined gradation and produces FOD-generating scaling/spalling; adjust mixture proportions and finishing technique to minimize hand finishing.
sections.body: Excessive hand finishing or adding mortar and water to the surface of the pavement are indicators of mixtures with an undesirable combined gradation. Continuing these practices produces pavements that are FOD generators, such as scaling and spalling. Adjust mixture proportions and finishing techniques whenever necessary to minimize hand finishing.
key_points: Excessive hand finishing / adding mortar-water is a symptom of poor combined aggregate gradation
Continuing the practice produces FOD-generating distresses (scaling, spalling)
Fix the mixture proportions and finishing technique rather than compensating with more hand finishing
sections.applicability: Applies to diagnosing chronic hand-finishing needs as a mixture-gradation problem, especially on airfields (FOD risk).

sections.title: Concrete Texturing
sections.summary: Texture provides water-escape paths and tire-surface sharpness (but does not prevent hydroplaning), applied while the concrete is still plastic; the following subsections cover brush/broom, wire combing, and wire tining methods.
sections.body: Concrete pavements require a surface texture that provides the desired level of skid resistance. The primary functions of surface texture are to provide paths for water to escape from beneath tires, and a degree of sharpness at the surface necessary for the tire to break through the residual film remaining after bulk water leaves. Concrete texturing is the most common technique used to provide a high skid-resistant pavement surface; however, texturing will not prevent hydroplaning. Texturing is applied while the concrete is still in plastic condition, via the methods covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Texture functions: water escape paths under tires, and surface sharpness to break through the residual water film
Texturing does NOT prevent hydroplaning
Applied while the concrete is still plastic
sections.applicability: Introduces the surface texturing method subsections that follow.

sections.title: Brush or Broom Finish
sections.summary: Applied transversely once bleed water sheen disappears, producing uniform ~1.5 mm (1/16 in.) deep corrugations without tearing; burlap drag (the most common airfield technique) targets a 1 mm (0.04 in.) mean macrotexture depth (ASTM E965) using ~500 gm/m2 (15 oz/yd2) burlap kept moist/clean with a heavy trailing-edge grout buildup.
sections.body: Brush/broom finish is applied when the water sheen (bleed water) has just disappeared, applied transversely across the pavement, producing corrugations that should be uniform in appearance and about 1.5 mm (1/16 in.) deep; the textured surface must not exhibit tears and be unduly rough. Burlap or Astroturf drag finish: macrotexture of the finished concrete surface should have a mean depth of 1 mm (0.04 in.) when measured by ASTM E965. Burlap drags are the most common texture technique for airfield pavements; burlap rating should be about 500 gm/m2 (15 oz/yd2), the trailing edge must have a heavy buildup of grout to produce the desired longitudinal striations, the drag must be operated with fabric moist and clean (or changed as needed to keep clean), and corrugations produced by burlap drag must be uniform and about 1.5 mm (1/16 in.) deep.
key_points: Applied once bleed water sheen disappears; corrugations uniform, ~1.5 mm (1/16 in.) deep
Burlap drag: most common airfield technique; target mean macrotexture depth 1 mm (0.04 in.) per ASTM E965
Burlap rating: ~500 gm/m2 (15 oz/yd2); keep fabric moist/clean with heavy trailing-edge grout buildup
sections.applicability: Applies to brush/broom and burlap-drag texturing, the default airfield texture method.

sections.title: Wire Combing (Rigid Steel Wires)
sections.summary: Wire combing provides deeper plastic-concrete texture via ~100 mm (4 in.) long, 0.8 mm (0.03 in.) thick, 2 mm (0.08 in.) wide steel wires, forming ~3 mm x 3 mm (1/8 x 1/8 in.) tracks spaced 13 mm (0.5 in.) center-to-center; no prior brush/broom/burlap finish is needed, and it is not a substitute for grooving (no drainage benefit).
sections.body: Use wire combing to provide a deeper texture in the plastic concrete. Steel wires are about 100 mm (4 in.) long, 0.8 mm (0.03 in.) thick, and 2 mm (0.08 in.) wide; continuous tracks are approximately 3 mm by 3 mm (1/8 in. by 1/8 in.) and spaced 13 mm (0.5 in.) center to center. Brush, broom, or burlap finish is not necessary before providing wire tining. Wire combing is not a substitute for grooving -- it does not provide for improved surface drainage.
key_points: Steel wire dimensions: ~100 mm (4 in.) long, 0.8 mm (0.03 in.) thick, 2 mm (0.08 in.) wide
Track dimensions: ~3 mm x 3 mm (1/8 x 1/8 in.), spaced 13 mm (0.5 in.) center-to-center
Not a substitute for grooving -- provides no drainage improvement
sections.applicability: Applies when a deeper plastic-concrete texture is specified via rigid wire combing.

sections.title: Wire Tining (Flexible Steel Bands)
sections.summary: Wire tining uses flexible steel bands ~130 mm (5 in.) long, ~6 mm (0.25 in.) wide, spaced 13 mm (0.5 in.) apart to provide a deep plastic-concrete texture; no prior brush/broom/burlap finish is required, and it is likewise not a substitute for grooving.
sections.body: Use wire tining to provide a deep texture in the plastic concrete. Flexible steel bands are about 130 mm (5 in.) long, approximately 6 mm (0.25 in.) wide and spaced 13 mm (0.5 in.) apart. Brush, broom, or burlap finish is not necessary before providing wire combing. Wire tining is not a substitute for grooving -- it does not provide for improved surface drainage.
key_points: Flexible steel band dimensions: ~130 mm (5 in.) long, ~6 mm (0.25 in.) wide, spaced 13 mm (0.5 in.) apart
Not a substitute for grooving -- provides no drainage improvement
sections.applicability: Applies when a deep plastic-concrete texture is specified via flexible wire tining.

sections.title: Guidance for Texturing and Grooving
sections.summary: The designer selects the texture type; burlap drag is the default if unspecified. Artificial turf, wire comb, and surface grooving textures are prohibited on airfield paving projects.
sections.body: The designer must select the type of texturing desired. If no guidance is given, the usual default method is burlap drag. For airfield paving projects, do not specify artificial turf, wire comb, or surface grooving textures.
key_points: Default texture if unspecified: burlap drag
PROHIBITED on airfield paving: artificial turf, wire comb, and surface grooving textures
sections.applicability: Governs which texture types may be specified for airfield paving projects.

sections.title: Grooving
sections.summary: Spring tine grooving is roads/streets only; airfield grooving must be sawcut (FAA standard or trapezoidal pattern). Standard grooves are ~6x6 mm (0.25x0.25 in.) at 37 mm (1.5 in.) spacing for airfields (50 mm/2 in. for roads); trapezoidal grooves are 57 mm (2.25 in.) spacing, 6 mm deep, 6 mm wide at bottom, 12 mm wide at top; grooves avoid runway centerline/joints/lights/cables and compression seals, and terminate 1.5-3 m (5-10 ft) from the pavement edge.
sections.body: Spring tine grooving is limited to use on roads and streets only. Grooving of airfield pavement must be sawcut, using either the FAA's standard or trapezoidal grooving patterns. For the standard groove pattern, grooves are approximately 6 mm by 6 mm (0.25 in. by 0.25 in.) and spaced 37 mm (1.5 in.) center to center for airfield pavements, and 50 mm (2 in.) for roads. Trapezoidal grooves are spaced 57 mm (2.25 in.) center to center, 6 mm (0.25 in.) deep, 6 mm (0.25 in.) wide at the bottom, and 12 mm (0.5 in.) wide at the top. Do not groove within 152 mm (+/-76 mm) (6 in. [+/-3 in.]) of the runway centerline, crown, transverse joints, working cracks, or light fixtures; do not groove within 6.1 m (20 ft) of the aircraft arresting system cable. Grooves are not required to cross joints; do not groove through compression seals, and replace any compression seals cut or otherwise damaged by grooving. Terminate grooves within 1.5 to 3 meters (5 to 10 feet) of the pavement edge to allow for operation of the grooving equipment.
key_points: Airfield grooving must be sawcut (FAA standard or trapezoidal pattern); spring tine grooving is roads/streets only
Standard pattern: ~6x6 mm (0.25x0.25 in.) grooves at 37 mm (1.5 in.) spacing for airfields, 50 mm (2 in.) for roads
Trapezoidal pattern: 57 mm (2.25 in.) spacing, 6 mm deep, 6 mm wide at bottom, 12 mm wide at top
Avoid grooving within 152 mm (+/-76 mm) of runway centerline/crown/joints/lights, or within 6.1 m (20 ft) of arresting cable
Never groove through compression seals (replace any damaged seal); terminate grooves 1.5-3 m (5-10 ft) from the pavement edge
sections.applicability: Governs airfield pavement grooving pattern, dimensions, and exclusion zones for skid resistance.

sections.title: Concrete Curing
sections.summary: Curing maintains adequate moisture/temperature after finishing; improper curing causes near-term plastic shrinkage cracking and long-term durability/warping problems. Four keys: proper mixing, uniform application, correct timing, and yield (coverage rate) verification.
sections.body: Curing is the maintenance of adequate moisture and temperature regimes in freshly placed concrete for a period of time immediately following finishing. Improper curing can have serious detrimental effects on near-term (plastic shrinkage cracking) and long-term properties of hardened concrete (less durable surface, excessive warping). Four important keys to proper application of a curing material are: (a) proper mixing, (b) uniformity of application, (c) timing of application, and (d) yield check (rate of application).
key_points: Improper curing causes near-term plastic shrinkage cracking and long-term durability/warping problems
Four keys: proper mixing, uniform application, correct timing, and yield (coverage rate) verification
sections.applicability: Introduces the curing-timing and curing-compound-spraying subsections that follow.

sections.title: Timing of Curing Application
sections.summary: Timing is critical, especially in hot weather; apply curing compound as soon as free water disappears from the surface after finishing/texturing (note: fly ash/slag mixtures may not show visible free water).
sections.body: Timing is critical, especially during hot weather. Apply curing compound as soon as free water disappears from the concrete surface after finishing and texturing. When using fly ash and slag, free water may not form.
key_points: Apply curing compound as soon as free water disappears from the surface (critical in hot weather)
Fly ash/slag mixtures may not show visible free water -- do not wait for a visual cue that will not appear
sections.applicability: Applies to timing the first application of curing compound after finishing/texturing.

sections.title: Curing Compounds Spraying
sections.summary: Spray curing uses self-propelled, lane-spanning equipment (hand spray only for hand-placed areas) with overlapping two-coat coverage; verify uniformity visually (white-pigmented) and by measured application-rate volume; apply to exposed faces after slipforming/form removal and to joint surfaces immediately after sawing/cleaning; moist curing must keep the entire surface continuously wet (typically 7 days) until a compound is applied.
sections.body: Uniform coverage and coverage rates are critical for sprayed curing compounds. Apply spray curing using spray equipment mounted on a self-propelled frame that spans the paving lane, limiting hand spray curing to hand-placed concrete areas. Employ overlapping coverage that provides a two-coat application. White-pigmented curing compound uniformity is subject to visual examination, but verify application rates by measuring the volume used for a given area against specification. Apply curing to exposed concrete faces after slipforming or removing forms, and to joint surfaces immediately after sawing and cleaning. If using moist curing, maintain the entire concrete surface continuously wet for the entire curing period (typically seven days) or until a curing compound is applied.
key_points: Self-propelled, lane-spanning spray equipment; hand spray limited to hand-placed areas
Overlapping two-coat coverage; verify both visually (white pigment) and by measured application-rate volume
Apply to exposed faces after slipforming/form removal, and to joints immediately after sawing/cleaning
Moist curing: keep the surface continuously wet, typically for 7 days, until a compound is applied
sections.applicability: Applies to spray-applied and moist curing compound operations.

sections.title: Minimizing Edge Slump
sections.summary: Edge slump is excessive if >15% of a slab's joint length exceeds 6 mm (0.15 in.) edge slump, or any edge slump exceeds 10 mm (3/8 in.); minimize occurrences (impacts joint efficiency/performance), stop paving and correct if continual correction in fresh concrete is leading to unacceptable joint spalling.
sections.body: Detect excessive edge slump while concrete is in the plastic state. Edge slump is considered excessive if more than 15 percent of the joint length for a single slab exhibits edge slump greater than 6 mm (0.15 in.), or if any edge slump exceeds 10 mm (3/8 in.). Minimize edge slump occurrences because it impacts joint efficiency and performance; continual correction of excessive edge slump in fresh concrete can lead to unacceptable levels of joint spalling in the finished concrete. If such a problem develops, stop paving and implement measures to correct excessive edge slump. Factors that affect edge slump include: concrete consistency; concrete mixture compatibility with placement techniques; paver adjustments and operation; and excessive finishing. The correction of edge slump is discussed in Chapter 11.
key_points: Excessive edge slump: > 15% of joint length exceeding 6 mm (0.15 in.), OR any point exceeding 10 mm (3/8 in.)
Continual fresh-concrete correction of edge slump risks unacceptable joint spalling later -- stop paving if this occurs
Contributing factors: concrete consistency, mixture-technique compatibility, paver adjustment/operation, excessive finishing
Edge slump correction/repair is discussed in Chapter 11
sections.applicability: Defines the numeric edge-slump acceptance criteria and when to halt paving to address it.

sections.title: Fixed Form Paving
sections.summary: Fixed form paving is typically used for short lengths/isolated areas (fillets, irregular pavements) via machine or manual placement; the following subsections detail form setting, transitions, damage prevention, and edge curing.
sections.body: Fixed form paving is typically used to pave short lengths or isolated areas such as fillets or irregular pavements and employs machine pavers or manual placement. Important considerations are covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Fixed form paving is used for short lengths/isolated/irregular areas via machine or manual placement
sections.applicability: Introduces the fixed-form paving subsections that follow.

sections.title: Steel Forms
sections.summary: Position forms on the finished base and check top elevations; low/high grade correction depends on base type (granular vs. stabilized), with special care taken not to correct only near the forms, which would create variable pavement thickness away from the forms.
sections.body: Position forms on the finished base and check top elevations, per the granular- and stabilized-base subsections that follow.
key_points: Position forms and check top elevations on the finished base before paving
Grade correction approach depends on whether the base is granular or stabilized
sections.applicability: Introduces the granular-base and stabilized-base form-setting subsections that follow.

sections.title: Granular Base
sections.summary: For low grade along granular-base forms, place/compact additional base material; for high grade, rework the base down; correcting only near the forms (not between them) leaves the pavement thinner away from the forms.
sections.body: If grade along the forms is low, place and compact additional base material. If grade along the forms is too high, rework the base to lower the grade. Correcting high spots in granular material only near form edges is poor practice -- high spots between the forms will result in a lower concrete thickness away from forms, producing variable thickness.
key_points: Low grade: add and compact additional granular base material
High grade: rework the base to lower it
Never correct high spots only near the forms -- fix high spots across the whole panel to avoid variable pavement thickness
sections.applicability: Applies to grade correction along fixed forms set on a granular base.

sections.title: Stabilized Base
sections.summary: For low grade on stabilized base, shim forms (up to 25 mm/1 in.) or remove/replace base; for high grade, cut down cement-treated/asphalt-stabilized open-graded bases with a motor grader, or grind lean concrete/asphalt concrete bases; a bond-breaker layer helps in ground areas.
sections.body: If grade along forms is low, shim forms to maintain horizontal alignment during concrete placement; if more than 25 mm (1 in.) shimming is needed, remove and replace the base in low areas to achieve the required base elevation. For high areas in cement treated base, cut down cement-treated open graded and open graded asphalt stabilized bases with a motor grader blade; grind high areas in lean concrete (econocrete) and asphalt concrete bases to elevation. Lowering base elevations only in the vicinity of forms results in a thin concrete cross-section away from forms that produces variable thickness. Consider a bond breaker layer of broadcast sand or double application of waxed-based curing compound in areas that are ground, to reduce the potential for bonding between the base and the concrete.
key_points: Low grade: shim forms up to 25 mm (1 in.); beyond that, remove/replace the base
High grade: motor-grader-cut cement-treated/open-graded asphalt-stabilized bases; grind lean concrete/asphalt concrete bases
Never correct only near the forms -- causes variable thickness away from them
Use a bond-breaker (broadcast sand or double waxed curing compound) in ground areas to prevent base-slab bonding
sections.applicability: Applies to grade correction along fixed forms set on a stabilized base.

sections.title: Set Forms
sections.summary: Mechanically tamp forms and stake them securely into the base, with stakes no more than 900 mm (36 in.) apart.
sections.body: Mechanically tamp forms and stake them securely into the base with stakes no more than 900 mm (36 in.) apart.
key_points: Mechanically tamp and securely stake forms into the base
Maximum stake spacing: 900 mm (36 in.)
sections.applicability: Applies to setting fixed forms before concrete placement.

sections.title: Check Transition Joints
sections.summary: Ensure no significant deviation affects finished concrete smoothness between forms.
sections.body: Ensure that no significant deviation affects the finished concrete smoothness between forms. Transition joint mismatches between adjoining fixed-form sections telegraph directly into rideability defects in the finished slab.
key_points: Verify no smoothness-affecting deviation exists between adjoining forms
Transition joint checks occur after forms are set, before concrete placement begins
sections.applicability: Applies to checking transition joints between adjoining fixed-form sections.

sections.title: After Forms are Connected
sections.summary: Check vertical and horizontal alignment after forms are connected.
sections.body: Check vertical and horizontal alignment. This final check, performed once forms are connected and before concrete placement, catches any misalignment introduced during form staking and tamping.
key_points: Verify vertical and horizontal alignment once forms are connected
This check follows form tamping/staking and precedes transition-joint verification
sections.applicability: Applies to final alignment checks immediately after connecting fixed forms.

sections.title: Damage
sections.summary: Spray forms with form release oil not more than four hours before paving, to minimize damage during form removal.
sections.body: To minimize damage during form-removal operations, spray forms with form release oil not more than four hours before paving.
key_points: Apply form release oil no more than 4 hours before paving to minimize form-removal damage
sections.applicability: Applies to timing form release oil application ahead of fixed-form paving.

sections.title: Spalling
sections.summary: Do not remove forms earlier than 12 hours after placement (to prevent corner spalling/damage); remove no later than 24 hours, since later removal may affect vertical-edge curing.
sections.body: To prevent corner spalling and damage to concrete, forms are not normally removed earlier than 12 hours after concrete placement; however, remove forms no later than 24 hours. Removing forms later than 24 hours may affect concrete curing of vertical edges adjacent to forms.
key_points: Form removal window: not earlier than 12 hours, not later than 24 hours after placement
Removal later than 24 hours can compromise vertical-edge curing
sections.applicability: Governs the acceptable time window for fixed-form removal.

sections.title: Exposed Sides
sections.summary: Spray exposed sides with curing compound within 30 minutes of form removal, at the same coverage rate used for the pavement surface.
sections.body: Spray exposed sides with curing compound within 30 minutes after form removal. Coat edges at coverage rates used for the pavement surface.
key_points: Apply curing compound to exposed sides within 30 minutes of form removal
Use the same coverage rate on exposed edges as on the pavement surface
sections.applicability: Applies to curing exposed vertical edges immediately after fixed-form removal.

sections.title: Paving and In-Pavement Structures
sections.summary: Introduces in-pavement lighting fixture guidance covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: This section covers in-pavement structures, primarily lighting fixtures, detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: Introduces in-pavement lighting-fixture guidance (Section 8-13.1)
sections.applicability: Introduces the lighting-fixture subsections that follow.

sections.title: Lighting Fixtures
sections.summary: Light cans are the most common in-pavement airfield structure; layout minimizes joint interference, with a blockout normally required when a light-base centerline falls within 750 mm (2.5 ft) of a pavement joint; installation techniques (blockouts, split cans/coring, cookie cutter) are covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: The most common in-place structures in airfield concrete paving are light cans. Layout in-pavement lighting systems to minimize interference with proposed pavement joints; for conflicts with pavement joints, make use of pavement blockouts to construct in-pavement lighting structures near a joint. Normally, a blockout is required when the centerline of the light base can is within 750 mm (2.5 ft) of a pavement joint. Light cans may be installed using the techniques detailed in the following subsections.
key_points: Light cans are the most common in-pavement airfield structure
Blockout normally required when a light-base centerline is within 750 mm (2.5 ft) of a joint
Installation techniques: blockouts, split cans/coring, cookie cutter (see following subsections)
sections.applicability: Applies to laying out and installing in-pavement light cans relative to pavement joints.

sections.title: Blockouts
sections.summary: Install blockouts at light can locations, pave around them, check for grout box clearance, keep filler material within 75 mm (3 in.) of finish elevation, then remove filler, position light cans, and backfill with concrete; fixed blockouts can restrain slab movement, so deformed tie bars around diamond-shaped blockouts hold restraint cracks tight.
sections.body: Install blockouts at light can locations and place the pavement around the blockouts. Check blockout elevations for grout box clearance. Place filler material used to stabilize blockouts within 75 mm (3 in.) or less of the finish elevation. After construction, remove any filler material, position light cans, and backfill the blockout area with concrete. Fixed blockouts can restrain slab movement and increase restraint stresses associated with moisture and thermal changes; use deformed tie bars around diamond-shaped blockouts to hold any restraint cracks tight and reduce the potential for crack spalling, positioning tie bars between the upper third and half depth of pavement, securely tied to chairs fastened to the base.
key_points: Keep blockout filler material within 75 mm (3 in.) of finish elevation
Fixed blockouts increase restraint stress -- use deformed tie bars around diamond-shaped blockouts
Tie bars positioned between the upper third and half slab depth, tied to base-fastened chairs
sections.applicability: Applies to the blockout method of installing in-pavement light cans.

sections.title: Split Cans and Coring
sections.summary: A 6-step technique: position/anchor a partial can, pave the lane, drill a 100 mm (4 in.) core to find the can center, drill a 360-460 mm (14-18 in.) hole for the top section, then complete installation.
sections.body: This technique allows the pavement to be slipformed with pre-placed light cans; can elevation adjustments can be made after concrete placement. Steps: (1) position partial can in the base; (2) pre-place concrete at the base of the partial cans to anchor them; (3) pave the lane; (4) drill a 100 mm (4 in.) diameter core to determine the exact center of the can; (5) drill a 360 to 460 mm (14 to 18 in.) hole for the can top section; (6) complete light can installation.
key_points: Split cans/coring allows slipforming over pre-placed, partially anchored light cans
Core drill diameter to find can center: 100 mm (4 in.)
Top-section hole diameter: 360-460 mm (14-18 in.)
sections.applicability: Applies to the split-can/coring method of installing in-pavement light cans under slipform paving.

sections.title: Cookie Cutter
sections.summary: Similar to coring: after the paver passes, a worker on a suspended bridge presses a 'cookie cutter' into the plastic concrete over an anchored light base; once set enough to hold shape but still finishable, the cutter is removed, the impression's concrete discarded, and the area hand finished.
sections.body: This technique is similar to the coring method: light cans are anchored in place and paving is placed over them. Steps: (1) after the paving machine passes over a light base, a 'cookie cutter' is pressed into the plastic concrete by a worker sitting on a bridge suspended over the pavement; (2) after the concrete sets (sufficiently rigid for the reservoir to retain its shape but plastic enough to allow surface finishing), the cookie cutter is removed, the concrete inside the impression is removed and discarded, and the surrounding surface is hand finished.
key_points: A worker on a suspended bridge presses a 'cookie cutter' into plastic concrete over an anchored light base
Timing: concrete must be rigid enough to hold the impression shape but still plastic enough to finish
The impression's concrete is removed/discarded and the area hand finished
sections.applicability: Applies to the cookie-cutter method of installing in-pavement light cans under slipform paving.

sections.title: Implications of Improperly Installed Light Bases
sections.summary: Checking light base height before paving is cheap; after paving, an incorrectly high light base has no fix but removal/replacement, so height verification is critical before concrete placement. Distorted uniformity around light bases (unknown root cause) can also block the light beam and is only detectable after paving.
sections.body: Benefits to the paving contractor include time and cost savings when light base installation deficiencies are detected before concrete paving; it is relatively cost free to check a light base before paving, but expensive to remove a light base after the pavement is placed and finished. The height setting of a light base is the most common cause of a deficient installation; when the light base is set too high, there is no satisfactory mitigation other than to remove and replace it, so checking height before concrete paving is a critical step. On some projects, the uniformity of the concrete surface surrounding the light base has been observed to distort to the extent that height tolerances become difficult to establish and high spots block the light beam; the specific cause(s) of this problem are not known and the condition is only detected during inspection after paving is complete. The surface around light base locations must be carefully inspected immediately after pavement finishing, while the concrete is still plastic.
key_points: Light base height is the most common installation deficiency; too-high bases have no fix but removal/replacement
Checking height before paving is cost-free; correcting after paving is expensive
Surface distortion around light bases (unknown cause) can block the light beam -- inspect while the concrete is still plastic
sections.applicability: Emphasizes pre-paving inspection of light base height and surrounding surface condition.

sections.title: Other Structures
sections.summary: Hydrant pits, utility manholes, and drainage trenches (via blockout or pre-placed methods) need embedded steel for crack control; larger structures stay >=1.2 m (4 ft) from joints (or get thickened-edge/expansion details if not feasible), smaller penetrations can sit closer (like light fixtures), and an isolation joint plus load-transfer detail is needed at the structure.
sections.body: Other in-place structures commonly encountered with airfield pavements include hydrant pits, utility manholes, and drainage structures (trenches); these are typically installed using the blockout method or pre-placed with concrete around the structure. In both cases, embedded steel must be used around the structure for crack control. Additional considerations: design details must account for pavement expansion adjacent to the structure and moisture infiltration into the structure; larger structures must be located at least 1.2 m (4 ft) from a transverse or longitudinal joint to minimize cracking potential -- if infeasible, place the structure at the pavement joint with appropriate load transfer (thickened edge) and slab expansion details; smaller slab penetrations (monitor wells, under-drain cleanouts) can be located closer to joints, similar to in-pavement light fixtures (no less than 750 mm [2.5 ft] from the joint); an isolation joint around an in-place structure must accommodate slab expansion, with load transfer between the slab and structure also accounted for; and trench drain walls must be designed stiff enough to resist pavement expansion, with struts potentially required if expansion movement is anticipated to be high.
key_points: Embedded steel is required around all in-place structures (hydrant pits, manholes, drainage trenches) for crack control
Larger structures: >= 1.2 m (4 ft) from joints, or thickened-edge/expansion details if that's infeasible
Smaller penetrations (monitor wells, cleanouts): >= 750 mm (2.5 ft) from joints, like light fixtures
Isolation joints and load-transfer details are required at in-place structures; stiff trench-drain walls (with struts if needed) resist expansion
sections.applicability: Applies to designing/constructing pavement around hydrant pits, manholes, and drainage structures.

sections.title: Paving at Flexible Pavement Interfaces
sections.summary: Matching elevations is a common problem where concrete abuts flexible (asphalt) pavement; techniques for a smooth interface are covered in the following subsection.
sections.body: Matching elevations is a common problem where concrete and flexible pavement sections abut one another.
key_points: Elevation matching is the core challenge at concrete-to-flexible-pavement interfaces
sections.applicability: Introduces the interface-smoothing techniques detailed in the following subsection.

sections.title: Techniques for a Smooth Interface
sections.summary: Sawcut the flexible pavement full-depth at the interface (shore it if pre-cut well ahead of paving, or over-cut and replace with a buried tied slab); compact the base at the interface, start paving from the flexible edge outward, avoid tracking slipform equipment on unsupported flexible edges, and manage cross-slope elevation matching via grinding, overbuild-and-resurface, or careful roller operation.
sections.body: Techniques for a smooth interface: sawcut flexible pavement vertically full depth where it abuts new concrete to minimize disturbance to the base layer under the asphalt; if the flexible system is sawcut significantly ahead of paving, shore up the vertical face to minimize loss of base from unsupported granular layers sloughing; alternatively, over-cut the flexible pavement, pave along the planned interface, and replace the flexible pavement at the over-cut (if possible, use a buried concrete slab tied to the concrete pavement along the over-cut area); to minimize faulting potential at the interface construction joint, compact the base adjacent to forms and along the cut flexible pavement edge using pole tampers and plate compactors; to minimize hand-finishing effort when matching elevations, start paving at the flexible pavement edge and move the paver away from the edge; do not allow slipform equipment to track on unsupported flexible pavement edges; and when paving parallel to the flexible pavement and matching elevations, depending on cross-slope drainage requirements, consider grinding the flexible pavement down to the planned concrete elevation, or placing concrete higher and thin-milling/resurfacing the flexible pavement -- during compaction of the asphalt surface layer, do not allow the steel roller to run on the concrete edge.
key_points: Sawcut the flexible pavement full-depth at the interface; shore the face if cut well ahead of paving
Alternative: over-cut, pave along the planned interface, then replace flexible pavement (optionally with a buried tied slab)
Compact the base at the interface with pole tampers/plate compactors to minimize faulting
Never track slipform equipment on unsupported flexible pavement edges; never roll the steel roller onto the concrete edge
sections.applicability: Applies to constructing a smooth, faulting-resistant transition between concrete and flexible (asphalt) pavement.

sections.title: Hot-Weather Concrete Placement
sections.summary: ACI defines hot weather as >3 consecutive days with average daily air temp > 25 C (77 F), or air temp >= 30 C (86 F) for more than half of any 24-hour period; the following subsection details mixture and practice adjustments.
sections.body: ACI defines hot weather as a period longer than three consecutive days exhibiting: the average daily air temperature greater than 25 C (77 F) (mean of the highest and lowest temperatures from midnight to midnight); or the air temperature for more than one-half of any 24-hour period not less than 30 C (86 F).
key_points: ACI hot weather definition: > 3 consecutive days with average daily air temp > 25 C (77 F)
OR: air temp >= 30 C (86 F) for more than half of any 24-hour period
sections.applicability: Establishes the numeric threshold that triggers hot-weather concreting procedures.

sections.title: Concrete Mixture
sections.summary: Use only a hot-weather mixture verified by trial batches cast at representative hot-weather temperatures; likely problems include rapid slump loss, reduced air content, premature stiffening, plastic shrinkage cracking, and thermal cracking.
sections.body: Only use a concrete mixture for hot weather previously verified as appropriate by using trial batches mixed and cast at temperatures representative of typical hot weather conditions for the site. During hot weather, problems that are likely to occur include: rapid slump loss; reduced air contents; premature stiffening; plastic shrinkage cracking; and thermal cracking.
key_points: Hot-weather mixtures must be trial-batch-verified at representative site hot-weather temperatures
Likely hot-weather problems: rapid slump loss, reduced air content, premature stiffening, plastic shrinkage cracking, thermal cracking
sections.applicability: Applies to qualifying a mixture design specifically for hot-weather placement.

sections.title: Hot Weather Concreting
sections.summary: Key hot-weather measures: stay within w/cm/dosage limits, use verified retarders, substitute slower-hydrating SCMs, increase AEA dosage, keep plastic concrete temp <=32 C (90 F) via cooled/SSD aggregates and chilled water/ice, use light-colored equipment, consider nighttime placement, moisten the base, cure/protect quickly (white compound, fog spray), and use the ACPA Evaporation Rate Calculator or HIPERPAV to trigger fog spray/retardant above 1.0 kg/m2/hr (0.2 lb/ft2/hr) evaporation, stopping paving if conditions are too severe.
sections.body: Hot weather concreting measures: do not exceed the maximum allowable w/cm ratio or the manufacturer's maximum recommended admixture dosage; use retarding admixtures if their performance is verified during trial batches (high dosages of water reducers, even high-range, can retard setting); substitute slag, Class F fly ash, or natural pozzolans for part of the cement, since these hydrate more slowly and generate lower heat of hydration; correct air content by increasing air-entraining admixture dosage; keep plastic concrete temperature as low as practical, not exceeding 32 C (90 F) -- aggregates may be sprinkle-cooled (correcting for aggregate moisture) and must be batched in a saturated surface dry condition; hot cement/fly ash from the supplier should not be used; mixing water may be chilled or chipped ice substituted for some water (ensure all ice melts during mixing); mixing/transporting equipment may be painted white/light to reduce solar heat absorption; concrete placements can be scheduled for nighttime; moisten the base before placement to keep its temperature down and prevent it absorbing water from the concrete; place/finish rapidly and apply curing compound (white, to reflect heat) at the earliest possible time, using fog spray or evaporation retardant if application is delayed; and reduce the rate of evaporation, since plastic shrinkage cracking likelihood increases with evaporation rate (a function of air temperature, concrete temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed) -- calculate evaporation rate with the ACPA Evaporation Rate Calculator or HIPERPAV software using current on-site weather data, and provide fog spraying or an approved evaporation retardant when the predicted rate exceeds 1.0 kg/m2/hr (0.2 lb/ft2/hr). If conditions are too severe to prevent plastic shrinkage cracking, or corrective measures are ineffective, stop paving until weather improves. Refer to ACI 305, Hot Weather Concreting, for additional information.
key_points: Max plastic concrete temperature target: 32 C (90 F); use SSD/cooled aggregates and chilled water/ice as needed
Substitute slag/Class F fly ash/natural pozzolans to reduce heat of hydration; verify retarder dosage by trial batch
Evaporation rate trigger for fog spray/retardant: > 1.0 kg/m2/hr (0.2 lb/ft2/hr), calculated via ACPA calculator or HIPERPAV
Stop paving if conditions are too severe to prevent plastic shrinkage cracking or corrective measures fail
Reference: ACI 305, Hot Weather Concreting
sections.applicability: Provides the operational procedures and numeric thresholds for placing concrete in hot weather.

sections.title: Cold Weather Concrete Placement
sections.summary: ACI cold weather = >3 consecutive days with average daily air temp < 4 C (40 F), or air temp <=10 C (50 F) for more than half of any 24-hour period; measures include higher cement content, reduced/eliminated slow SCMs (unless needed for ASR/sulfate), lower AEA dosage, verified Type C/E accelerators, no chloride admixtures, ice/snow-free aggregates, mixed concrete temp >=10 C (50 F) via heated (<66 C/150 F) water/aggregate, no placement below 4 C (40 F) air/surface temp, freeze protection ready before starting, maintaining >=10 C (50 F) for 72 hours then above freezing until 20 MPa (3,000 psi), and removing/replacing any freeze-damaged concrete.
sections.body: Cold weather is defined by ACI as a period when, for more than three consecutive days: the average daily air temperature is less than 4 C (40 F) (mean of highest/lowest from midnight to midnight); or the air temperature is not greater than 10 C (50 F) for more than one-half of any 24-hour period. When concrete is to be placed in cold weather, or when cold weather is likely, plans to maintain appropriate concrete temperature must be made well before temperatures are expected to drop below freezing.
