Considerations: cold-weather mixture designs normally have higher cement content than hot-weather mixes; reduce/eliminate slag, fly ash, and pozzolans unless required for ASR/sulfate resistance (in which case increase total cementitious content or use Type III instead of Type I/II cement); required air-entraining admixture dosage should be lower than at normal temperatures; concrete takes longer to set, so plastic shrinkage cracking risk exists (especially if the concrete is much warmer than ambient air or the wind is blowing); an accelerating admixture (ASTM C494/CRD-C 87 Type C or E) may be used if trial-batch-verified; do NOT use admixtures containing added chlorides, or calcium chloride; aggregates must be free of ice, snow, and frozen lumps before mixing; mixed concrete temperature should equal or exceed 10 C (50 F), with mixture water/aggregates heated to less than 66 C (150 F) and evenly heated; do not place concrete when air or placement-surface temperature is less than 4 C (40 F); covering/protection from freezing must be available before starting placement; maintain concrete temperature at 10 C (50 F) or above for at least 72 hours after placement and above freezing for the remainder of curing (until 20 MPa [3,000 psi] compressive strength) -- corners/edges are most vulnerable to freezing; completely remove and replace concrete damaged by freezing; cold-weather concrete (especially with SCMs) gains strength slowly, so joint sawing may be delayed and in-place strength should be verified by maturity method, temperature-matched curing, nondestructive testing, or core tests before opening to traffic. Refer to ACI 306, Cold Weather Concreting, for additional information.
key_points: ACI cold weather: > 3 consecutive days with average daily air temp < 4 C (40 F), or <= 10 C (50 F) for over half of any 24-hour period
Mixed concrete temperature target: >= 10 C (50 F); heat water/aggregates to < 66 C (150 F), evenly heated
No placement when air or surface temperature is below 4 C (40 F); NO chloride-containing admixtures or calcium chloride
Maintain concrete >= 10 C (50 F) for 72 hours, then above freezing until reaching 20 MPa (3,000 psi)
Verify in-place strength (maturity method, temperature-matched curing, NDT, or cores) before opening cold-cured concrete to traffic
sections.applicability: Provides the operational procedures and numeric thresholds for placing concrete in cold weather.

sections.title: Protecting Concrete Against Rain Damage
sections.summary: Protective coverings must be on-site at all times; batching/placing stops when rain begins, fresh concrete gets covered, and various guidance covers surface-imprint/paste-washout risk, rapid-cooling thermal-restraint risk, water-removal/dry-cement prohibitions, and using early-entry/skip sawing to beat incoming rain.
sections.body: The paving team and inspector must know procedures to protect fresh concrete from rain: protective coverings (polyethylene sheeting, tarpaulins) must be available on-site at all times; when rain starts, batching/placing should stop and fresh concrete must be covered so rain does not indent the surface or wash away cement paste. Two primary rain consequences: surface damage (imprints, washed-away paste, generally minimal once final set is achieved); and rain-induced rapid surface cooling after final set, which can accelerate thermal restraint stress development and increase early-age uncontrolled cracking risk even with timely sawcutting (see Chapter 9). Should a rainstorm occur before the curing membrane is effective, damage is usually surface-limited; stiff, low-slump, consolidated/struck-off/finished concrete may sustain only minor surface blemishes from light rain, and light rain will not soak in enough to raise the effective w/cm ratio. Compromised texture from light rain can generally be repaired by diamond grinding to about 3 mm (1/8 in.) depth. Concrete exposed to significant rain while loose/unconsolidated must NOT be used in the pavement, since it can absorb water. Once the unprotected surface is exposed to rain, do not attempt to finish or texture it; do not attempt to remove extra surface water before covering (this increases paste erosion); and do not add or float dry cement into the surface (extends exposure time and can alter the entrained air-void system). As soon as the surface dries, apply the curing membrane; once curing is complete, diamond-grind rain-exposed surfaces to remove blemishes and re-texture. Any attempt to finish/texture during or after the rain event risks working water into the surface, worsening a minor problem. Unconsolidated concrete exposed to rain that was incorporated into the pavement must be removed. Consider early entry saws or skip sawing to quickly install joints before incoming rain, since prompt joints reduce early-age cracking potential from rapid surface cooling. Once rain has ceased and coverings are removed, saw needed joints as quickly as possible. If a rainstorm catches unprotected pavement, stop paving immediately -- larger airfield projects may rely on on-site weather stations or forecasting services to anticipate weather.
key_points: Protective coverings must be on-site at ALL times; stop batching/placing and cover fresh concrete when rain starts
Concrete exposed to significant rain while loose/unconsolidated must NOT be incorporated into the pavement
Never remove surface water before covering, and never add/float dry cement into a rain-affected surface
Light rain damage is generally repairable by diamond grinding to ~3 mm (1/8 in.) depth
Consider early-entry saws or skip sawing to install joints quickly ahead of incoming rain
sections.applicability: Applies to protecting fresh concrete from and responding to rain events during paving.

sections.title: Assessing Rain Effects
sections.summary: Rain severity assessment ranges from beneficial light mist, through surface-accumulating water (stop paving, protect), to hard rain that marks fresh concrete (stop paving immediately), each with its own subsection.
sections.body: Consider the following guidelines in assessing rain effects, covered in the subsections below: mist, accumulated water, and hard rain.
key_points: Rain severity spans mist (may be benign) through accumulated water to hard rain (stop paving)
sections.applicability: Introduces the rain-severity assessment subsections that follow.

sections.title: Mist
sections.summary: An intermittent light mist may be beneficial, as long as no significant water is added to the unconsolidated concrete in front of the paver or to the surface being finished.
sections.body: An intermittent light mist may be beneficial, as long as no significant water is added to the unconsolidated concrete in front of the paver or to the concrete surface to be finished.
key_points: Light intermittent mist can be beneficial if it adds no significant water to unconsolidated concrete or the finishing surface
sections.applicability: Applies to distinguishing benign light mist from rain requiring corrective action.

sections.title: Accumulated Water
sections.summary: If rain accumulates any water at all on the surface of freshly placed concrete before finishing, stop paving and take protective measures.
sections.body: If rain is sufficient to accumulate any water at all on the surface of freshly placed concrete prior to finishing, stop paving and take protective measures.
key_points: Any water accumulation on fresh concrete before finishing triggers stopping paving and protective action
sections.applicability: Applies to identifying the accumulated-water threshold that requires halting paving.

sections.title: Hard Rain
sections.summary: If rain is sufficiently hard to mark freshly placed concrete, it is past time to stop paving.
sections.body: If rain is sufficiently hard to mark freshly placed concrete, it is past time to stop paving. At this severity, the paving team should already be executing the protective-covering procedures described in Section 8-18, not still assessing whether to stop.
key_points: Rain hard enough to mark fresh concrete means paving should already have stopped
Hard rain is the most severe rain-assessment category, beyond mist and accumulated water
sections.applicability: Applies to identifying the most severe rain threshold, past which paving must have already stopped.

sections.title: Testing Rain-Exposed Surface
sections.summary: Evaluate rain damage extent; remove not-durable (abrasion/skid/freeze-thaw) surface, using cores from the damaged surface's beginning/end for petrographic examination of surface hardness/air-void system alteration; general non-durability threshold for abrasion is >3 mm (1/8 in.) damage depth, and freeze-thaw durability requires air-void spacing factor < 0.20 mm (0.008 in.).
sections.body: Evaluate any rain damage and establish the extent of damage. Rain-damaged concrete must be removed if the surface is determined to be not durable in terms of abrasion, skid resistance (surface texture), or freezing and thawing. Cores can be drilled for petrographic examination to determine if rain has altered the surface hardness or entrained air-void system; recover cores from the beginning and end of the damaged surfaces. Results from the petrographic examination can establish the limits of and disposition of damaged concrete. Generally, surfaces are not deemed durable for abrasion if damage extends down more than 3 mm (1/8 in.); for freeze-thaw durability, the air-void spacing factor should be less than 0.20 mm (0.008 in.). Other tests assess scaling and abrasion potential.
key_points: Remove rain-damaged concrete found not durable for abrasion, skid resistance, or freeze-thaw
Petrographic cores from the beginning/end of damaged areas establish limits and disposition
Abrasion non-durability threshold: damage depth > 3 mm (1/8 in.)
Freeze-thaw durability requires air-void spacing factor < 0.20 mm (0.008 in.)
sections.applicability: Applies to evaluating and disposing of concrete surface damage after a rain event.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Guide
sections.summary: Common job-site problems and possible remedies are described in Table 8-2 (Troubleshooting Placement, Finishing, Texturing, Curing).
sections.body: Common problems encountered at the job site and possible remedies are described in Table 8-2, spanning premature stiffening, slump/air variability, failure to set, sticky mix, honeycombing, edge slump, smoothness problems, popouts, scaling/dusting, plastic shrinkage cracking, random cracking, raveling, joint spalling, and low-strength samples -- each with probable causes and corrective actions.
key_points: Table 8-2 is a full diagnostic guide: problem -> probable cause(s) -> corrective action
Covers stiffening/setting problems, slump/air variability, honeycombing, edge slump, smoothness, popouts, scaling, cracking, raveling, spalling, and low-strength samples
